q: In a circular motion, the object just moves in a circle.
e:
This is the definition of circular motion as stated in
the textbook.

q:
Artificial satellites going around the earth at a
constant height is an example of circular motion.
e: Satellites moving at a constant height follow a circular path.

q: In rotational motion, the object rotates about an axis.
e:
Rotational motion is characterized by rotation around a fixed
axis.

q:
The rotation of the earth about its own axis creates the cycle
of day and night.
e:
This is a provided example
of rotational motion.

q:
The motion of a Ferris wheel in an amusement
park is an example of circular motion only.
e:
The textbook lists the motion of a Ferris wheel as an example of rotational
motion.

q:
A rigid body is a body that deforms or changes shape when it
moves.
e:
A rigid body is defined as a body
that does not deform or change shape.

q:
In a rigid body, the distance
between any two particles within the body remains constant.
e:
This constant distance is the defining characteristic of a rigid
body.

q:
If a rigid body is in rotational motion, all the particles
constituting it undergo circular motion about a common axis.
e:
All particles in a rotating rigid body follow circular paths
around the shared axis of rotation.

q:
When an object rotates, it can
speed up or slow down.
e:
Rotation speed is not
necessarily constant; it can vary over time.

q:
If the angular velocity
of a rotating object is changing, it has an angular acceleration.
e:
Angular acceleration is defined as the rate of change
of angular velocity.

q:
If angular velocity changes at a constant rate,
the angular acceleration is constant.
e:
Constant angular acceleration occurs when the change in angular velocity is
uniform over time.

q:
The motion is called rotational motion under
constant angular acceleration if the angular velocity changes at a variable
rate.
e:
It is only called constant angular
acceleration if the rate of change is constant.

q:
Angular
displacement, angular velocity, and angular acceleration are considered
rotational variables.
e:
These variables are
used to analyze rotational motion.

q:
The kinematic equations for
rotational motion can be derived in terms of angular displacement, angular
velocity, and angular acceleration.
e:
These
three variables are the components of rotational kinematic equations.

q:
The symbol \omega_0 represents the initial angular speed of an object at
t = 0.
e:
\omega_0 is the standard notation for
initial angular velocity/speed.

q:
The constant angular acceleration is
defined by the formula \alpha = \frac{\omega - \omega_0}{t}.
e:
Angular acceleration is the change in angular velocity
divided by time.

q:
The equation \omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t
relates angular velocity to time and acceleration.
e:
This is equation (1.1) for rotational motion under constant angular
acceleration.

q:
Average angular speed is calculated as
\bar{\omega} = \frac{\omega - \omega_0}{2}.
e:
Average angular speed is the sum of initial and final speeds divided by 2:
\bar{\omega} = \frac{\omega + \omega_0}{2}.

q:
Angular
displacement \theta for a time interval t is expressed as
\theta = \bar{\omega} t.
e:
Angular
displacement is the product of average angular speed and time.

q:
The
equation for angular displacement under constant angular acceleration is
\theta = \omega_0 t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2.
e:
This is the standard kinematic equation (1.3) for rotational
displacement.

q:
The equation
\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2 \alpha \theta relates angular velocity,
acceleration, and displacement.
e:
This is
equation (1.4) for rotational motion.

q:
The equations of motion for
constant angular acceleration are entirely different from those for linear
motion.
e:
The equations are analogous, where
linear quantities are replaced with corresponding angular ones.

q:
In
the analogy between linear and angular motion, linear displacement s corresponds
to angular displacement \theta.
e:
Table 1.1
shows s and \theta are corresponding quantities.

q:
In the analogy
between linear and angular motion, linear velocity v corresponds to angular
acceleration \alpha.
e:
Linear velocity v
corresponds to angular velocity \omega.

q:
The unit of angular
acceleration in the textbook examples is rad \ s^{-2}.
e:
Radians per second squared is the standard SI unit for angular
acceleration.

q: One revolution (1 \ rev) is equal to 2\pi \ rad.
e:
A full circle is 2\pi radians, which equals
one revolution.

q:
The angular acceleration of a rotating object is
equal to zero if the object is at rest or rotating at constant angular
velocity.
e:
If \omega does not change, then
\alpha = 0.

q:
If a ball starts from rest and reaches
25 \ rad \ s^{-1} after traversing 41 \ rad, its angular acceleration is
7.62 \ rad \ s^{-2}.
e:
Using
\omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2 \alpha \theta: 25^2 = 0 + 2(\alpha)(41), so
\alpha = 625/82 \approx 7.62 \ rad \ s^{-2}.

q:
According to
Example 1.1, if a Ferris wheel reaches 1.5 \ rad \ s^{-1} in 10 \ s, its
angular acceleration is 0.15 \ rad \ s^{-2}.

If an object has
an angular acceleration of 0.15 \ rad \ s^{-2}, it will complete exactly 2
revolutions in 10 \ s starting from rest.
e: Example 1.1 shows it completes 1.19 \ rev in 10 \ s.

q:
Angular
velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement with respect to time.
e:
This is the definition of angular velocity
provided in Exercise 4.

q:
A body undergoes circular motion if it
rotates about its own internal axis.
e:
That
defines rotational motion; in circular motion, the object moves along a circular
path.

q:
Rotational motion under constant angular acceleration is
analogous to linear motion under constant acceleration.
e:
The textbook explicitly maps the kinematic equations of one to the
other.

q:
The formula \omega = \frac{\omega + \omega_0}{2}
represents the instantaneous angular velocity.
e: This formula represents the average angular speed \bar{\omega}.

q:
If initial angular velocity is zero, angular displacement is simplified to
\theta = \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2.
e:
When
\omega_0 = 0, the first term in \theta = \omega_0 t + \frac{1}{2}\alpha t^2
becomes zero.

q:
All particles of an object rotating around the axis of rotation
move in a circular path.
e:
This is a
fundamental property of a rotating rigid body.

q:
All particles of a
rotating body move in circles lying on planes parallel to the axis of
rotation.
e:
The planes are perpendicular to
the axis of rotation, not parallel.

q:
The center of rotation for every
particle in a rotating rigid body lies on the axis of rotation.
e:
The axis of rotation is the common center for all the
circular paths of the particles.

q:
The relation between arc length s
and angular displacement \theta is s = r\theta, where \theta is measured in
degrees.
e:
The angle \theta must be measured
in radians for the formula s = r\theta to be valid.

q:
The
instantaneous angular velocity \omega is different for different particles of a
rotating rigid body.
e:
The instantaneous
angular velocity is the same for all particles comprising the object.

q:
The relation between linear velocity v and angular velocity \omega is
v = r\omega.
e:
Linear velocity is the product
of the radius and the angular velocity.

q:
In the relation
v = r\omega, \omega must be measured in radians per second.
e:
Standard units (radians) are required for these
rotational-linear relationships.

q:
The direction of linear velocity
for a particle in rotational motion is tangent to its path.
e:
Linear velocity always acts along the tangent to the circular path
of the particle.

q:
Linear velocity in rotational motion is also called
radial velocity.
e:
It is called tangential
velocity because it is tangent to the path.

q:
If the magnitude of
angular velocity changes, the object will have a tangential acceleration.
e:
A change in angular speed results in a change
in linear speed, which is tangential acceleration.

q:
Tangential
acceleration a_T is always perpendicular to the circular path.
e:
Tangential acceleration is always tangent to the circular
path.

q:
The tangential acceleration a_T relates to angular
acceleration \alpha by the equation a_T = r\alpha.
e:
This is the correct relationship between linear and angular
acceleration.

q:
Tangential acceleration is a measure of how fast the
tangential velocity changes.
e:
This definition
is highlighted in the textbook's red box.

q:
The direction of the
angular velocity vector is parallel to the plane of rotation.
e:
The angular velocity vector is perpendicular to the plane of
rotation.

q:
The direction of angular velocity is usually specified by
the right-hand rule.
e:
The right-hand rule is
the standard convention for determining the vector direction.

q:
Using
the right-hand rule, if the fingers point in the direction of rotation, the
thumb points in the direction of the angular velocity vector.
e:
This is the correct application of the right-hand rule
described in the text.

q:
When angular velocity is increasing, the
angular acceleration vector points in the same direction as the angular
velocity.
e:
Acceleration and velocity vectors
align when the object is speeding up.

q:
When angular velocity is
decreasing, the angular acceleration vector points in the opposite direction to
the angular velocity.
e:
Acceleration and
velocity vectors are opposite when the object is slowing down.

q:
On a
rotating carousel, a child sitting halfway out from the center has a greater
linear velocity than a child on the outer edge.
e:
Since v = r\omega and \omega is constant, the child with the larger
radius (outer edge) has a greater linear velocity.

q:
All children on
the same rotating carousel have the same angular velocity, regardless of their
distance from the center.
e:
Angular velocity is
the same for every particle of a rotating rigid body.

q:
If a
merry-go-round has a radius of 5 \ m and rotates through an angular
displacement of 50 \ rad, the distance traversed is 250 \ m.
e: s = r\theta = 5 \times 50 = 250 \ m.

q:
The unit
of tangential acceleration is m \ s^{-1}.
e: The unit of acceleration (tangential or otherwise) is m \ s^{-2}.

q:
If a wheel of radius 0.2 \ m has an angular acceleration of
12 \ rad \ s^{-2}, its tangential acceleration is 2.4 \ m \ s^{-2}.
e: a_T = r\alpha = 0.2 \times 12 = 2.4 \ m \ s^{-2}.

q:
The
tangential acceleration vector points along the radius towards the center.
e:
The tangential acceleration vector is tangent
to the rim/path, not radial.

q:
For any particle in a rigid body, the
relation between tangential and angular quantities depends on its distance r
from the axis.
e:
Linear quantities (s, v, a_T)
are proportional to the radius r.

q:
Uniform circular motion describes an object moving in a circle at
a constant speed v.
e:
Constant speed in a
circular path is the definition of uniform circular motion.

q:
In
uniform circular motion, the velocity of the object is constant.
e:
Speed is constant, but velocity is not because its direction
is continuously changing.

q:
The continuous change in direction of
velocity in circular motion constitutes an acceleration.
e:
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, which includes
changes in direction.

q:
Centripetal acceleration points toward the
center of the circle.
e:
The term 'centripetal'
means center-seeking.

q:
Centripetal acceleration is also known as
radial acceleration.
e:
It is directed along the
radius, hence the name radial acceleration.

q:
The magnitude of
centripetal acceleration is given by a_c = \frac{v^2}{r}.
e:
This is the primary formula for centripetal acceleration in terms
of linear speed.

q:
Substituting v = r\omega into the centripetal
acceleration formula gives a_c = r\omega^2.
e:
This is the correct formula for centripetal acceleration in terms of angular
velocity.

q:
In uniform circular motion, the centripetal acceleration
and linear velocity vectors are parallel.
e: They are perpendicular; velocity is tangential while acceleration is radial.

q:
Nonuniform circular motion occurs when an object moves in a circular
path with a varying speed.
e:
Varying magnitude
of velocity (speed) defines nonuniform circular motion.

q:
In
nonuniform circular motion, the object experiences both tangential and
centripetal acceleration.
e:
Centripetal
acceleration accounts for direction change, and tangential acceleration accounts
for speed change.

q:
Centripetal acceleration is only present in
nonuniform circular motion.
e:
Centripetal
acceleration is present in both uniform and nonuniform circular motion.

q:
The resultant acceleration \bar{a} in nonuniform circular motion is the
vector sum \bar{a} = \bar{a}_c + \bar{a}_T.
e:
The total acceleration is the combination of the radial and tangential
components.

q:
The two acceleration vectors \bar{a}_c and \bar{a}_T
are perpendicular to each other.
e:
One is
radial (towards center) and the other is tangential (along path).

q: The magnitude of the resultant acceleration is a = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_T^2}.
e:
Since the components are perpendicular, the
Pythagorean theorem is used.

q:
The direction of the resultant
acceleration \bar{a} is given by \tan\phi = \frac{a_c}{a_T}.
e:
The correct formula is \tan\phi = \frac{a_T}{a_c} where
\phi is the angle with respect to the radial vector.

q:
If a hard
drive rotates at 7200 \ rpm, its angular speed is 240\pi \ rad \ s^{-1}.
e:
Conversion:
7200 \times \frac{2\pi}{60} = 120 \times 2\pi = 240\pi \ rad \ s^{-1}.

q:
In Example 1.4, a bit requires 0.5 \ \mu m of length; at a speed of
22.62 \ m \ s^{-1}, the writing rate is 4.52 \times 10^7 bits per second.
e:
Rate =
\frac{v}{length} = \frac{22.62}{0.5 \times 10^{-6}} = 4.52 \times 10^7
bits/s.

q:
A minus sign in angular acceleration indicates that the
rotating object is speeding up.
e:
A minus sign
indicates that the object is slowing down (decelerating).

q:
If
a_c \gg a_T, the magnitude of the resultant acceleration is approximately equal
to the centripetal acceleration.
e:
If one
component is much larger than the other, the resultant is dominated by the
larger component.

q:
A piece of food on a rotating microwave plate
experiences only centripetal acceleration when the plate rotates at a constant
angular velocity.
e:
At constant \omega,
\alpha is zero, so there is no tangential acceleration, only centripetal.

q:
When a microwave plate starts to spin faster, the food on it experiences
both tangential and centripetal acceleration.
e:
Spinning faster implies angular acceleration (\alpha 
eq 0), creating
tangential acceleration.

q:
Centripetal acceleration is produced in
circular motion because the direction of the velocity vector is constantly
changing.
e:
This is the fundamental reason for
the existence of centripetal acceleration.

q:
The tangential
acceleration of a centrifuge slowing down from 7200 \ rpm to rest in 30 \ s
with a radius of 0.2 \ m is -5.03 \ m \ s^{-2}.
e:
Calculated as
a_T = r\alpha = 0.2 \times (-8\pi) \approx -5.03 \ m \ s^{-2}.

q:
In uniform circular motion, the angular acceleration \alpha is equal to
zero.
e:
Uniform means constant angular speed,
so no angular acceleration exists.

q:
The centripetal acceleration
vector always points away from the center of the circular path.
e: It always points towards the center of the path.
